accepted.question_text: For the graph-model version of Isaacs' princess and monster game, where the searcher finds the hider once they are in the same place, solve the game on graphs other than the circle. In particular, determine the correct solution for the interval case, which the source says is not solved but only conjectured.

evidence.quote: The searcher then ﬁnds the hider once they are in the same place. This version of the princess and monster game was also proposed by Isaacs [11, p 349-350]. The game on a graph has only been solved for the circle (see Sect. 1.2 of this book), but it remains open for all other graphs. Even if the graph is an interval, although there is a conjectured solution in this case, which we will discuss below.

accepted.question_text: Can two lions catch a man in finite time in a bounded planar region containing rectifiable lakes, when all players have equal maximum speeds and capture requires the lion and the man to coincide?

evidence.quote: The princess and monster game is relat ed to the game between the lion and a Christian, which was invented by Richard Rado: a lion and a Christian in a closed circular arena have equal maximum speeds.Can the lion catch the Christian in ﬁnite time? Surprisingly, the answer turns out to be NO [3, p 46], provided that the players are both represented by points, and the radius of detection is zero.

Littlewood in his Miscellany [ 14], and he added the following problem: can two lions catch a man in a bounded area with rectiﬁable lakes? According to Béla Bollobás [ 3], this problem remains unsolved.

accepted.question_text: Consider the princess and monster game on the interval [-1,1], where the monster moves continuously with maximum speed 1 and the princess may relocate with unbounded speed. Let M1 be the monster strategy that chooses an arbitrary initial point and direction, runs to one endpoint, and then back to the other endpoint; let M2 be the strategy that again chooses an arbitrary initial point and direction, runs until meeting the sweeper coming from that direction, then turns around, joins that sweeper, and finally traverses to the other endpoint; and let P be the class of princess strategies that either stay at an endpoint or start at a point in [-1+ε,-ε]∪[ε,1-ε], wait until the nearest-end sweeper is ε-close, then run to the middle and back to an endpoint. Is it true that against any mixed strategy supported on M1∪M2 there exists an optimal princess response supported on P, so that the interval game reduces to the stated optimization problem?

evidence.quote: In [ 2] it has been conjectured that an optimal mixed strategy for M can be based upon the following pure strategies: M1 Choose an arbitrary initial point and an arbitrary direction. M runs in that di- rection until the end, and then back until the other end. M2 Again choose an arbitrary initial point and an arbitrary direction. But now M runs until he meets the sweeper coming from that direction, then turns around and runs until the end, joining the sweeper, and then back until the other end.

If the strategy space of the monster is restricted to these pure strategies, then the optimal mixed strategy of the princess is based upon the following pure strategies: P Choose an inﬁnitesimal ε > 0. Either hide at an end-point and remaind immo- bile, or choose an arbitrary initial point in [−1 + ε,−ε]∪[ε,1−ε] and remain

there until the sweeper that st arts from the nearest end point is ε-close. Then run to the the middle until ε-close, turn, and run back until the end. It is possible to show that there exists an optimal response in M1 ∪M2 against any mixed strategy that is based on P. The conjecture in [ 2] is that conversely against any mixed strategy that is based on M1 ∪M2 there exists an optimal response that is in P. If this conjecture is true, then the princess and monster game on an interval reduces to a standard optimization problem that can be solved numer- ically by discretization and linear programming.

accepted.question_text: For the princess and monster game on a tree, does there exist an optimal princess strategy with the confluency property that whenever two princess trajectories meet at some time t0, they coincide for all earlier times up to t0?

evidence.quote: one should observe the following nice conﬂuency property of the princess’ strategy : suppose that p1, p2 ∈P and that p1(t0)= p2(t0) for some t0.T h e np1(t)= p2(t) for all t0 ≥t

Perhaps it is possible to derive the optimal response of the monster from this property, and verify the conjecture. We conjecture more generally, that for the game on a tree there exists an optimal princess strategy that satisﬁes the conﬂuency property.

accepted.question_text: In Gilbert's high-low search game, Blue chooses a secret number h, after each guess tells Red whether the guess is too high, too low, or correct, and may then change the secret number provided the new choice remains consistent with all previous answers. If V(n) is the value of the n-number game, is it true that V(n) - log2(n) converges to a constant c as n→∞, with c approximately 0.487?

evidence.quote: Dresher’s guessing game has recently been solved asymptotically [8], but there is a very similar high-low search game that remains unsolved. It was proposed around the same time as Dresher’s game, by Ed Gilbert [ 12]. As in Dresher’s game, Blue chooses a secret number h and tells Red whether his guess is too high, too low, or correct. However, after doing this, Blue may change the secret number, but it has to be in accordance with the answers that have been given so far.

This recursion should make the game easier to solve. It certainly makes the value of the game easier to compute, and it is conjectured in [7] that the value of the game satisﬁes lim n→∞ V (n)−log2(n)= c for some constant c = 0.487 ... .

accepted.question_text: In the continuous high-low guessing game where Blue chooses h in [0,1], Red repeatedly guesses, is told whether each guess is too high or too low, and Blue's payoff is the infinite sum of the absolute errors Σ|g_n-h|, Steve Alpern found a pure minimax strategy for the searcher. Does there exist any mixed searcher strategy with strictly better performance than that known pure minimax strategy?
accepted.context_brief: Continuous guessing game: mixed vs pure searcher

evidence.quote: The following continous version of the game was ﬁrst proposed by Vic Baston and Fred Bo- stock: Blue chooses a secret number h ∈[0,1]. Red repeatedly guesses it and is told whether the guess is too high or too low (the probability of guessing the ex- act number is zero). If g n is the sequence of guesses, then Blue’s payoff is equal to ∑ |gn −h|.
S t e v eA l p e r n[1] found a pure minimax strategy for the searcher, see Fig 5.1.
However, it is unknown if there exists a mixed strategy that performs better.

accepted.question_text: In the same continuous high-low guessing game with h in [0,1], high/low feedback after each guess, and payoff Σ|g_n-h| to the hider, what is an optimal strategy for the hider?

evidence.quote: Blue chooses a secret number h ∈[0,1]. Red repeatedly guesses it and is told whether the guess is too high or too low (the probability of guessing the ex- act number is zero). If g n is the sequence of guesses, then Blue’s payoff is equal to ∑ |gn −h|.
An optimal strategy for the hider has never been determined.

accepted.question_text: Modify the continuous guessing game by allowing the hider to move from one secret number h_n to the next h_{n+1} between consecutive guesses, and score the hider by Σ|g_n-h_∞|, where h_∞ is the limiting value of the hider's secret numbers. The source states that Alpern's pure minimax strategy still works for this payoff. Can one prove that this pure minimax strategy is actually optimal for the moving-hider version of the game?

evidence.quote: One can modify the continuous guessing game following Gilbert, by allowing the hider to move from one secret number hn to the next hn+1 between consecu- tive guesses. There are various choices for the payoff: it could be either ∑ |gn −hn| or ∑ |gn −h∞|,w h e r eh∞ denotes the limiting value of the hider’s secret numbers.

Alpern’s pure minimax strategy still works for the payoff ∑ |gn −h∞ |, even though the hider has a larger strategy space. It should be easier to prove that the pure min- imax strategy is optimal in this case.

accepted.question_text: Consider the continuous high-low guessing framework restricted to two guesses, with payoff (g2-h)^2 to the hider. What are the optimal strategies in this two-guess quadratic-payoff game?

evidence.quote: Instead of ∑ |g n −h| one may also consider other norms or other payoffs. Tom Ferguson has studied a game with two guesses only, in which the payoff to the hider is (g2 −h)2. Despite its apparent simplicity, this game is non-trivial and the optimal strategies are not easy to ﬁnd, see [6].

accepted.question_text: In Dresher's guessing game on the set {1,2,...,n}, where Blue chooses a secret number and Red repeatedly guesses with too-high/too-low feedback, is Johnson's conjecture true that for n>4 the probability Blue assigns to the number 1 equals the total probability Blue assigns to the set {2,3}?

evidence.quote: Blue chooses h, an integer from the set 1 to n (a region to hide). Red guesses an integer from 1 to n, is told whether he is too high or too low, and repeats until he guesses h . The payoff to Blue is one unit for each guess.

Finally, we would like to mention the following conjecture of Johnson: in Dresher’s guessing game, the probab ility that Blue chooses the secret number 1 is equal to the probability that Bl ue chooses the secret number in {2,3},i f n > 4. This problem has remained unsolved for almost 50 years now, and may very well be the longest standing open problem on search games.
